title: Smell
subtitle: Training your nose
objectives: Judge the intensity of a wine's aromas
Sort aromas into primary, secondary and tertiary
Smell in a way that finds more aromas

steps.title: Intensity first
steps.body: Before naming aromas, judge how strong they are: light, medium or pronounced. Then ask what they remind you of. A young Sauvignon Blanc jumps out of the glass; a young Chardonnay from a cool place may be much quieter. Neither is better, but it tells you about the grape and style.

steps.title: Three families of aroma
steps.body: Primary aromas come from the grape and fermentation: fruit, flowers, herbs. Secondary aromas come from winemaking: vanilla and toast from oak, butter from malolactic, bread from lees. Tertiary aromas come from age: leather, mushroom, honey, nuts, dried fruit. Naming the family tells you how the wine was made and how old it is.

steps.prompt: Vanilla and toast in a wine usually come from:
steps.explanation: Vanilla and toast are secondary aromas from oak barrels. Bottle age gives tertiary notes like leather and honey instead.

steps.title: How to smell
steps.body: Swirl to lift aromas, then take short sniffs rather than one long one; your nose tires within seconds. Start with broad groups, like fruit or flowers, then narrow down: red fruit, then strawberry or cherry. Smelling real fruit, herbs and spices at home is the fastest way to build your vocabulary.

steps.prompt: Which of these are tertiary aromas, from age?
steps.explanation: Dried fruit, leather and mushroom develop with years in bottle or barrel. Fresh lime and green apple are primary fruit.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Primary aromas come from the grape, secondary from winemaking, tertiary from age
Short sniffs, broad to narrow, build skill fastest
